ground_truth_core_content:
Introduction:
**0:** The generated intro covers the same high-level thesis as the expected section (moving beyond single monolithic LLM calls toward modular patterns, previewing chaining/parallelization/routing/orchestrator-worker), but it is missing the expected section's actual substantive hook: the "common trap" of treating LLMs as black boxes, the specific debugging failure mode ("you have no idea which of the 20 instructions in your mega-prompt was the weak link"), and the emphatic "This is not real engineering" declaration. In its place, the generated section substitutes a recap of Lessons 1-4, which is not present in the expected introduction at all. A similar black-box/debugging idea does appear later in the generated article's own "Challenge" section, but per the rule that each section must stand entirely on its own, that cannot credit this section. BORDERLINE: the shared high-level thesis is real, and a grader who treats the "trap" framing as decorative rather than substantive would score this 1 instead.

The Challenge with Complex Single LLM Calls:
**1:** Both sections cover the same core problems with single monolithic calls (black-box debugging difficulty, lack of modularity, lost-in-the-middle, higher token cost/lower reliability) and walk through the same practical example: Gemini client setup, three mock renewable-energy webpages combined into one string, a single complex prompt asking for FAQs with sourced answers, a sample output, and a closing point that single-source citation errors creep in as complexity grows. The generated section's setup code adds an `env.load(...)` call not shown in the expected article text, but this matches the actual lesson notebook's real setup cell (confirmed in the golden notebook content) and is additive, not a substitution of a different named artifact. One softer point: the expected section's example output visibly demonstrates the single-source-citation error it is making (attributing an answer that spans two sources to only one), while the generated section's chosen example output is itself correctly and fully sourced, so the argument about citation misses is asserted in prose rather than shown - the idea is still stated, so this alone does not drop the score to 0.

The Power of Modularity: Why Chain LLM Calls?:
**1:** Both sections introduce prompt chaining as connecting sequential LLM calls / a divide-and-conquer strategy, and cover the same four benefits (modularity, accuracy, debugging, flexibility/model-mixing e.g. cheap model for classification + powerful model for generation) and the same downside cluster (latency, cost, engineering/error-handling complexity, information loss when a task is split). The generated section's information-loss sentence ("splitting tasks can sometimes remove the context that connects them") is a reasonable paraphrase of the expected section's "some instructions lose their intended meaning when separated" point rather than a clean omission.

Building a Sequential Workflow: FAQ Generation Pipeline:
**1:** Both sections cover the same 3-step breakdown (generate questions -> answer questions -> find sources), the same three function definitions, combining them into a sequential_workflow, and the same measured execution time (22.20 seconds matches the expected section and the actual notebook output exactly). The generated section compresses the Pydantic/QuestionList/SourceList class definitions into code-comment placeholders rather than showing them explicitly; since this is an implementation-detail compression consistent with the guideline's own "no production code" and "don't reintroduce Lesson 4 (structured outputs)" constraints rather than a removed idea, it is treated as accepted compression, not a content gap.

Optimizing Sequential Workflows With Parallel Processing:
**1:** Both sections cover the same optimization rationale (independent per-question work can run concurrently), the asyncio/event-loop explanation for why LLM calls are good async candidates, the process_question_parallel + parallel_workflow functions, the same measured time improvement (22s -> 8.98s, matching the expected section exactly), and the same rate-limit caution. The generated section's rate-limit handling advice is thinner than the expected section's (which lists exponential backoff, Retry-After headers, and dynamic concurrency), but the guideline explicitly asks this section to "stay brief" on detailed rate-limit handling, so the thinner treatment is guideline-consistent rather than a dropped idea - the core notion (rate limits will trigger errors your application must handle) is still present.

Introducing Dynamic Behavior: Routing and Conditional Logic:
**1:** Both sections cover the need for routing when inputs require different processing, LLM-as-classifier/dispatcher, the divide-and-conquer/single-responsibility rationale, and both use the billing-vs-technical-support framing the guideline asks this section to preview. The expected section's aside about routing to different LLM models (a forward-reference to a future lesson) is absent from the generated section. BORDERLINE: that aside is explicitly marked as a tangent in the expected article and is not called for by the guideline's own bullet list for this section, so it reads as supplementary rather than core - but a stricter reading of "all ideas present in the expected section" would score this 0 for the omission.

Building a Basic Routing Workflow:
**0:** Both sections cover classify_intent as an LLM classifier constrained to a fixed category list, per-intent specialized prompts, and a handle_query router with a fallback branch. However, the expected section demonstrates this with two worked examples - a technical-support query and a billing query - each showing a different intent correctly classified and routed, while the generated section carries through only the technical-support example and drops the billing example entirely. REVISED per ruling: the guideline's "stay brief on detailed query examples/outputs" instruction governs how much detail to give the examples that are kept, not whether to keep all of the examples the expected section uses to demonstrate that the router generalizes across intent types - dropping an entire worked example is a missing substantive idea, not compression, so this scores 0.

Orchestrator-Worker Pattern: Dynamic Task Decomposition:
**1:** Both sections cover the orchestrator dynamically decomposing a multi-part customer query (billing + return + status) into typed sub-tasks, dispatching each to a specialized worker, and a synthesizer combining the results into one coherent reply, with the flexibility-vs-parallelization distinction (subtasks aren't predefined) called out in both. The generated section describes the worker functions and the final synthesized email in prose rather than showing the worker stub code or the full email text the expected section includes; the guideline explicitly asks this section to stay brief on "detailed worker function logic" and "detailed complex query example and output," so this compression is guideline-consistent rather than a dropped idea.

Conclusion:
**0:** Both sections recap the same four patterns (chaining, parallelization, routing, orchestrator-worker) and both close by previewing the next lesson. However, the expected section explicitly previews two future lessons - Lesson 6 (Agent Tools & Function Calling) and Lesson 7 (Planning & Reasoning, with a description of reasoning/planning capabilities) - while the generated section previews only the tools/function-calling lesson and never mentions a planning/reasoning follow-on at all. This is a full missing idea (an entire forward-reference), not a formatting difference, so it drives the score to 0 even though the rest of the section matches well.
